analysis.title: The Netherlands defies Europe's tech trend thanks to ASML
key_insights: The Netherlands is an exception in Europe in capturing the global tech boom, because of ASML and the semiconductor-equipment cluster around it. The IMF's latest World Economic Outlook lists the Netherlands among the countries most exposed to the global AI investment cycle through trade.

ING estimates ASML's direct contribution to Dutch GDP rose from 0.1% in 1995 to 1.3% in 2025 and could reach 1.6% in 2026. The 2026 figure uses the midpoint of ASML's own turnover guidance of €44.5bn.

Including domestic suppliers and investment, ING estimates ASML's total contribution to Dutch value-added could reach 2.2% in 2026. The total for ASML plus the wider machinery industry was 3.7% in 2025.

ASML accounts for about half of Dutch machinery industry turnover (€33.7bn in 2025, vs 47% in 2024). The machinery industry's share of Dutch gross value-added reached around 2.7% in current prices and 2.9% in constant prices by 2025.

For each euro of ASML turnover, about 50 cents is value-added from its own activities, and ING assumes 40 cents of that is domestic. Intermediate consumption adds 0.3% of Dutch value-added in 2025 (0.4% forecast for 2026), and investment adds 0.2% in both 2025 and 2026.

ASML is the sole producer of leading-edge lithography tools, which gives it strong pricing power in negotiations. TSMC has recently shown reluctance to adopt ASML's newest technology, initially viewing the tools as too costly, which shows the pricing power has limits.

ING flags concentration risk: ASML's business is cyclical, so semiconductor swings can increasingly affect Dutch growth. ASML's growing services business for its installed base is typically less cyclical and partly offsets this.

The Nokia comparison: Nokia was close to 4% of Finnish GDP around 1998-2000 (3.8% in 2000, excluding indirect effects) and fell to 0.5% by 2011. ING argues the Netherlands is more diversified, with pharma and IT services also contributing to growth.

Geopolitical fragmentation is a two-way risk. US restrictions already limit exports of ASML's most advanced machines to China, and the proposed Match Act could constrain Dutch exports further. Foreign inputs depend on Germany, Taiwan, South Korea and the US.

Domestic supply constraints (talent, space, other bottlenecks) are the main concern for further cluster growth despite the Dutch government's 2024 decision to invest €2.5bn in the business climate. ING still expects the ASML cluster to remain an important structural driver of Dutch growth.
ASML has rapidly become the largest European company by market capitalisation, and changes in its turnover expectations have become informative for the Dutch near-term economic outlook.

sector_views.rationale: ING describes ASML and the equipment cluster as a structural driver of Dutch growth, benefiting from the global AI investment cycle. The note is an economic analysis, not a formal sector rating.

earnings_insights: ASML guidance: ING uses the midpoint of ASML's own 2026 turnover projection, €44.5bn, from the most recent quarterly press release (company guidance, not a reported figure).

ASML turnover was €33.7bn in 2025 (ING cites this as about half of Dutch machinery industry turnover; reported basis not further specified). Dutch machinery industry turnover was €60.6bn in 2024, and Statistics Netherlands put Dutch chip industry turnover at €42.5bn in 2024 on a new ad hoc definition.

macro_indicators.indicator: ASML direct contribution to Dutch GDP (value-added share)
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING estimate rather than an official statistic. It is up from 0.1% in 1995 and shows ASML is a macro-relevant company for the Netherlands.

macro_indicators.indicator: ASML direct contribution to Dutch GDP (value-added share)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Based on the midpoint of ASML's own guidance of €44.5bn and ING's growth forecasts.

macro_indicators.indicator: ASML total contribution including suppliers and investment
macro_indicators.interpretation: Direct plus indirect effects. The Netherlands' growth is increasingly tied to semiconductor cycle swings.

macro_indicators.indicator: Machinery industry plus ASML total impact on Dutch value-added
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING estimate. It compares with Nokia's 3.8% share of Finnish GDP in 2000, excluding indirect effects.

macro_indicators.indicator: Machinery industry share of Dutch gross value-added
macro_indicators.interpretation: The share has risen since 2017 and accelerated with the AI investment cycle.

risk_factors: Concentration risk: Dutch growth is increasingly exposed to the cyclical semiconductor industry and one company.
Geopolitical restrictions on export markets and disruption of critical foreign inputs, such as ZEISS SMT optics from Germany.
Domestic bottlenecks in talent, space and other supply-side factors could limit cluster growth.
Customer pushback on pricing, as in TSMC's initial reluctance to adopt ASML's newest tools on cost.
Possible permanent damage from a shock to a dominant firm, as in Nokia's decline and Finland's productivity slowdown.
charts_described: Chart: share of the machinery industry in total Dutch gross value-added, rising since 2017 to around 2.7% in current prices by 2025.
Chart: estimated ASML cluster impact on Dutch gross value-added, expected to grow to 2.2% in 2026.
geopolitical: US restrictions already limit exports of ASML's most advanced machines to China.
The proposed Match Act could constrain Dutch chip equipment exports further.
Export demand is exposed to disruptions involving the US, Germany, China and South Korea, per IMF analysis.
Foreign intermediate inputs for Dutch machinery depend on Germany, Taiwan, South Korea and the US.

tension_points.bull_case: ASML and its ecosystem lift Dutch value-added (2.2% in 2026 including indirect effects), cushion shocks and drive productivity spillovers. Services revenue from the installed base is less cyclical.
tension_points.bear_case: Dependence on one cyclical company creates concentration risk, as the Nokia case in Finland shows. Geopolitical restrictions and domestic talent and space limits could stall growth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A shock to ASML's competitive position of the kind Nokia suffered with smartphones, or export restrictions that sharply cut access to key markets.

theme_stances.key_argument: ASML and its ecosystem give the Netherlands a unique position in the AI investment boom and remain a structural driver of Dutch growth.
theme_stances.evidence: ASML has become a macroeconomic force in its own right

theme_stances.key_argument: Dependence on one company and exposure to export restrictions and foreign inputs create downside risk to Dutch growth.
